text: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid. Read that again. The last pharaoh of Egypt is closer to Neil Armstrong than to the pyramids. Our brains are terrible at judging time. Everything before our grandparents gets squashed into one blurry thing called 'the past'. So today, we're going to stretch history back out, and look at it at its true scale.
This is True Scale. Let's start with the pharaohs.

But first, a quick test. Without thinking too hard, which is closer to us today: Cleopatra, or the building of the Great Pyramid? And which lived closer in time to you: a T. rex, or a Stegosaurus? Hold on to your answers. By the end of this video, your sense of time is going to look very different.

The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around two thousand five hundred and seventy B.C. Cleopatra was born in sixty-nine B.C. That's a gap of about two and a half thousand years. Now jump forward from Cleopatra to Apollo eleven, in nineteen sixty-nine. That's only about two thousand years. By the time Cleopatra ruled, the pyramids were already ancient. Even the Greek historian Herodotus, writing around four centuries before she was born, described them as wonders from a distant age. And the Great Pyramid stayed the tallest structure humans had ever built for nearly three thousand eight hundred years.

And here's a twist. Cleopatra wasn't Egyptian by descent at all. Her family, the Ptolemies, were Greek-speaking Macedonians. They took over Egypt after Alexander the Great conquered it in three thirty-two B.C. By the time Cleopatra became queen, in fifty-one B.C., Greek rulers had held Egypt for about two hundred and eighty years. Ancient Egypt was so old that even its last dynasty was a foreign one.

Here's something even stranger. When the Great Pyramid was finished, woolly mammoths were still alive. Most of them had died out thousands of years earlier, but a small population survived on Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean, north of Siberia. The last of them disappeared around four thousand years ago. That's several centuries after the pyramid was built. So while Egyptians were carving hieroglyphs, mammoths were still walking the Earth.

Let's jump to the Middle Ages. Teaching at the University of Oxford had begun by ten ninety-six. The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, wasn't founded until thirteen twenty-five. That's more than two hundred years later. And the Aztec Empire itself only formed in fourteen twenty-eight, and fell to the Spanish in fifteen twenty-one. So Oxford is older than the Aztec Empire, and it's still teaching students today.

And while we're in that era, here's another overlap. The Roman Empire didn't end with the fall of Rome in the west. Its eastern half carried on from Constantinople for nearly another thousand years, until the city fell to the Ottomans in fourteen fifty-three. By then, Johannes Gutenberg was already printing with movable type in Germany. And just thirty-nine years later, Columbus sailed across the Atlantic. The Roman Empire lasted into the age of the printing press.

Now let's go much further back. We tend to picture all the dinosaurs living together. They didn't. Stegosaurus lived around a hundred and fifty million years ago. Tyrannosaurus rex appeared near the very end, around sixty-eight million years ago. That means about eighty million years separate Stegosaurus from T. rex. And only sixty-six million years separate T. rex from you. You are closer in time to a T. rex than a T. rex was to a Stegosaurus.

And here's one more from deep time. The earliest shark-like fish left their scales in rocks around four hundred and fifty million years old. The first trees appeared around three hundred and eighty-five million years ago. So shark-like fish were swimming in the oceans for more than sixty million years before there was a single tree on land.

Time plays tricks in the other direction too. Some things we think of as far apart actually overlapped. Abraham Lincoln and Charles Darwin were born on the very same day, the twelfth of February, eighteen oh nine. The fax machine was invented in eighteen forty-three, more than thirty years before the telephone. And Nintendo was founded in eighteen eighty-nine, as a playing card company, just a year after the Jack the Ripper murders in London.

Here's another pair that sounds like it belongs to different eras. Anne Frank and Martin Luther King Junior were both born in nineteen twenty-nine. We remember one from the Second World War, and the other from the civil rights movement of the nineteen sixties. If Anne Frank had survived, she would have been just thirty-four years old when King gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech.

Some of the past is much closer than it feels. France carried out its last execution by guillotine in September nineteen seventy-seven. By then, Star Wars had already been in American cinemas for months. The Wright brothers made the first powered flight in nineteen oh three. Just sixty-six years later, humans were walking on the Moon. Someone could have seen both, in one lifetime.

And here's the one that really collapses time. The American Civil War ended in eighteen sixty-five. Yet the United States was still paying a Civil War pension until twenty twenty. It went to Irene Triplett. Her father, Mose, had fought in that war, and was eighty-three years old when she was born, in nineteen thirty. She received seventy-three dollars and thirteen cents a month, until she died in May twenty twenty, at the age of ninety.

Part of the problem is that big numbers all sound the same. A million, a billion, a trillion. So let's turn them into time. A million seconds is about eleven and a half days. A billion seconds is nearly thirty-two years. Count back a billion seconds from today, and you land in the middle of the nineteen nineties. And a trillion seconds? Almost thirty-two thousand years. Count back a trillion seconds from today, and you're deep in the last Ice Age.

So let's finish with the biggest scale of all. Take the entire history of the universe, thirteen point eight billion years, and squeeze it into a single calendar year. The Big Bang happens at midnight on the first of January. Each day on this calendar is about thirty-eight million years. The Earth doesn't form until early September. The first signs of life appear in late September. The dinosaurs don't show up until Christmas Day, and they're wiped out on the thirtieth of December.

Now zoom into the last day. December the thirty-first. Our own species, Homo sapiens, appears at about eleven forty-eight p.m. Just twelve minutes before midnight. The Great Pyramid is built about ten seconds before midnight. Every empire you've ever read about, every war, every invention, from the pyramids to your phone, fits into those last ten seconds. And Columbus sailing to the Americas? Just over one second ago.

So next time something feels like ancient history, remember the true scale. Cleopatra is closer to us than to the pyramids. You are closer to a T. rex than a T. rex was to a Stegosaurus. And all of human history fits into the last few seconds of the cosmic year. If this made your head spin a little, subscribe to True Scale. And tell me in the comments which fact surprised you the most.
